_note: Per-app rule weightings. One review harness, three different problems.
A weight multiplies a finding's severity score. 0 suppresses the rule for that
app; 1.0 is neutral; above 1.0 promotes. The point is not tuning -- it is that
the same rule means different things in different codebases. `token-drift` in a
design system is the system failing; in a purchased marketing template it is a
report that the template is not our token file, which we already knew.
CORRECTNESS RULES CANNOT BE WEIGHTED DOWN. route.py clamps contrast,
touch-target, overflow and every *-indeterminate rule to a floor of 1.0 and
says so in the plan. That floor is the June 2026 ruling made mechanical: gates
adjudicate correctness and coverage, taste stays human. A profile that could
silently mute an accessibility failure would be a taste knob on a correctness
gate, which is the one thing this pipeline may not grow.

why: Next 14, purchased template. Its tokens are the vendor's, not ours, so
conformance findings against our token file are reports about provenance
rather than about quality. What actually matters on a landing page is the
judgement the deterministic layer cannot make: does the eye land in the
right place, does the page read as one thing. So the rules go quiet and
Next 16, React 19, Tailwind 4 + Panda. An internal operator tool with a
real token source, where drift IS the defect and the deterministic layer
does nearly all the work. The model is asked least here, because the
questions it answers are the ones this app has fewest of.
Its Tailwind engine has no declared token source (measured 2026-08-26:
zero @theme blocks in the app-shell CSS entry), so a K-family verdict on a
Tailwind-authored colour is an abstention, not a pass -- see PIPELINE_SPEC
1.0. That is a routing fact, not a weighting one, and it is why this app's
gestalt budget being low does not mean its VLM queue is empty.
Next 13, guest-facing but ours. Neither a vendor template nor a strict
system, so nothing is weighted away and nothing is promoted.
